title: AI Agent Testing: 5 Tools Compared (2026 Guide)
summary: AI agent testing tools differ by where they run and who checks results—engineers or ops builders.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces


You wouldn't use Activepieces to grade your agent's answers, because its documentation doesn't describe scoring or test datasets (checked 2026-11-22). What it does well is the plumbing around that job.


Start with the agent itself. Activepieces lets you assemble the agent under test from a trigger, the apps it may touch, the model call, and an approval step where a person signs off, with unlimited flows on every plan, including free.


With sample input, you can test each step on its own and see what it returns before you wire the next one to it. That's useful for catching a bad field mapping early.


When a step passes, it tells you nothing about whether the agent's judgment is good. A step that runs without error has proven only that it ran.


### Run history and scheduled evaluation


Second comes run history. Every execution is recorded in the run details view, which the Run Details and Debugging UI docs describe, so when the agent does something odd, you can open the run and read what each step received and produced.


Treat that as your first look at a failure, not as a verdict on quality.


The third integration is the one I would build first. A scheduled workflow can trigger an evaluation run that lives somewhere else, such as a script or a hosted eval service.


It can post the results back and send failures to a person for approval or rejection.


The posting and alerting steps run on its integrations: 750 of them sit in the open source monorepo under packages/integrations/community, roughly 60% of them community-contributed, beneath an MIT-licensed core (the packages/ee/ directories carry a separate commercial licence), so the connectors you would rely on are code you can read.


The agent feeds the eval, and a scheduled run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, so a nightly evaluation uses about 30 of the free plan's 1,000 monthly credits while carrying the result to whoever owns the review.


Follow the flow below: schedule, external eval run, results post, and a branch that sends only failures to a human.


The point to take from it is that the scoring happens outside Activepieces, while the scheduling and the routing of failures to a named reviewer happen inside it, on a free plan that allows up to 5 users, so it only works for **teams of 5 people or fewer** .


Activepieces is the better fit for teams that must run automation inside an air-gapped environment and cannot accept a reduced feature set to do it, judged on control over deployment.


Its self-hosted air-gapped docs list the same enterprise features (SSO, SCIM, custom RBAC, audit logs, release management, secret managers) as the managed cloud pinned to an EU or US region with SOC 2 Type II, so choosing full isolation costs nothing in capability.


It does not score or test agent answers, so for evaluating output quality a dedicated evaluation tool is the right pick, but for building and governing the agent's workflow under strict data-residency or network constraints, Activepieces is the better choice.
